books.section: Topic 4.13 The Society of the South in the Early Republic, A. Slavery and the Southern “Way of Life”

primary_sources: John C. Calhoun, "Slavery a Positive Good," Senate speech, February 6, 1837

stimulus.text:
John C. Calhoun, senator from South Carolina, speaking in the Senate on February 6, 1837, during debate over abolitionist petitions:

“But let me not be understood as admitting, even by implication, that the existing relations between the two races in the slaveholding States is an evil:—far otherwise; I hold it to be a good, as it has thus far proved itself to be to both, and will continue to prove so if not disturbed by the fell spirit of abolition.”

“I fearlessly assert that the existing relation between the two races in the South, against which these blind fanatics are waging war, forms the most solid and durable foundation on which to rear free and stable political institutions.”
stimulus.source_note: Quotations verbatim from John C. Calhoun, Senate speech, February 6, 1837, as printed on Wikisource (Slavery a Positive Good). Viewed and checked before writing.

source: original; stimulus verbatim from John C. Calhoun, Senate speech, February 6, 1837, public domain
stem: In the second passage, Calhoun argues that slavery provides what for Southern society?

options.text: A supply of cheap labor for Northern textile mills
options.misconception: Calhoun speaks of political institutions in the South, not of Northern mills.

options.text: A reason for the South to abandon plantation farming
options.misconception: Calhoun defends the plantation order; he never suggests abandoning it.

options.text: A way to end the debate over abolitionist petitions
options.misconception: Calhoun is answering the petitions, not ending debate about them.

options.text: The foundation for free and stable political institutions

rationales.A: Calhoun speaks of political institutions in the South, not of Northern mills.
rationales.B: Calhoun defends the plantation order. He never suggests abandoning it.
rationales.C: Calhoun is answering the petitions, not ending debate about them.
rationales.D: Calhoun calls slavery the most solid foundation for free and stable political institutions. He ties slavery to the very idea of Southern freedom.
rationales.general:
1. Find the claim. Calhoun calls the relation between the races the most solid foundation for free and stable political institutions.
2. Notice the move. He does not defend slavery as a regrettable need; he makes it the base of Southern freedom itself.
3. Test the options. Only one names a political foundation rather than a labor supply or an escape from debate.
Background: Calhoun was answering abolitionists who called slavery a sin, so he answered with a moral and political defense.
Remember: a writer can defend an institution by tying it to a value his audience already holds.
